enrichment.short_title: Gypsy caravan site refused in Green Belt
key_facts: The claimant sought planning permission to station three caravans and portaloos for Gypsy families on former playing-field land in Chessington within the Green Belt.
A planning inspector dismissed the appeal, finding the change of use inappropriate under PPG2 and no very special circumstances despite gypsy accommodation needs.
The claimant argued the inspector misapplied PPG2 and failed to treat the borough's non-compliant gypsy site policy CS5 as a material consideration under Circular 1/94.
Collins J held the inspector's approach was lawful and that even a non-compliant local plan would not have made this Green Belt development permissible.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review challenge to a planning inspector's decision dismissing an appeal against refusal of planning permission.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; respondent awarded costs of £3,250 after reduction for unnecessary document preparation.
enrichment.ratio: Where gypsy accommodation is sought in the Green Belt, the inspector must consider Circular 1/94 and individual need, but inappropriate development under PPG2 paragraph 3.12 remains inevitable if openness and Green Belt purposes would be harmed and no very special circumstances are shown; local plan non-compliance with Circular 1/94 does not of itself require permission.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector wrongly applied PPG2 paragraph 3.4 rather than 3.12
Whether failure to comply with Circular 1/94 in policy CS5 was a material consideration
Whether very special circumstances existed for gypsy accommodation in the Green Belt
Whether the inspector properly assessed individual and borough-wide gypsy need

confidence.notes: Full administrative judgment with detailed planning policy analysis and clear outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Blackmail conviction appeal after co-accused evidence
key_facts: The appellant was convicted of blackmail with his co-accused after demanding £750,000 from a vulnerable widow using a secretly recorded sexual video.
The co-accused pleaded guilty at the last moment and gave evidence for the Crown; £12,500 from the victim was found hidden at the appellant's home.
The appellant appealed on trial management grounds, including refusal to adjourn for envelope expert evidence, and on fresh prison witness evidence said to exonerate him.
The Court of Appeal found the judge's timetable control lawful and rejected the fresh evidence as not credible.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction and six-year sentence, with leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals against conviction and sentence dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A trial judge may refuse adjournment for speculative expert investigations without undermining fairness where no material was excluded by time pressure; fresh post-conviction evidence must be credible to render a conviction unsafe, and prison gossip unsupported by reliable corroboration does not meet that threshold.
legal_issues: Whether refusal of adjournment for envelope expert evidence made the conviction unsafe
Whether the trial was unfairly rushed
Admissibility and weight of late Spymaster and cash evidence
Whether fresh evidence from a fellow prisoner undermined safety of conviction
Whether six years' imprisonment was manifestly excessive

confidence.notes: Long full judgment covering trial conduct, evidential rulings, fresh evidence, and sentence with explicit conclusions.

key_facts: The claimant had a registered easement to draw water from a borehole on the defendant's land at Wood Dalling Hall, Norfolk.
The defendant owned the pump and filtration plant and ceased maintaining them, requiring the claimant to make alternative arrangements.
A recorder declared that repair and replacement costs should be borne rateably by volume among co-users of the borehole.
The Court of Appeal held no transmissible positive obligation to contribute existed under general easement law or quasi-contract.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from a recorder's declaration on borehole maintenance contributions between neighbouring landowners.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the recorder's declaration set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Apart from express covenant or special custom, the owner of a servient tenement is not obliged to repair apparatus needed to enjoy an easement of water; a blanket declaration imposing future rateable contribution on all co-users by volume cannot be justified by benefit/burden or quasi-contract where there is no implied request tied to specific expenditure.
legal_issues: Whether co-users must contribute to borehole pump repair and replacement costs
Application of Duke of Westminster v Guild and Rance v Elvin
Whether benefit/burden or quasi-contract supports a continuing contribution obligation
Whether a forward-looking rateable contribution declaration binds successors in title

confidence.notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on easement principles with clear reversal of the declaration.

enrichment.short_title: Hendrix settlement breach and Wrotham Park damages

statutes_considered.title: Dramatic and Musical Performers' Protection Act 1958

key_facts: PPX breached a 1973 settlement restricting exploitation of Jimi Hendrix master recordings by granting fresh licences in 1995 and 1999 of non-Schedule A material.
Buckley J granted injunctions but refused damages or an account of profits and accepted a limited accounting undertaking.
Experience Hendrix could not prove financial loss from the breaches but sought Wrotham Park-style damages or an account under Attorney General v Blake.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal in part, awarding a reasonable sum for breach but not a full account of profits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from High Court trial on remedies for breach of a 1973 recording settlement agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; PPX ordered to pay a reasonable sum for unauthorised use and to account by court order rather than limited undertaking.
enrichment.ratio: Following Blake and Wrotham Park, a deliberate breach of a negative contractual restriction may attract damages measured by the benefit the wrongdoer reasonably should have paid even without proved financial loss, but an account of all profits is exceptional and not warranted in an ordinary commercial licensing context; injunctive relief for the future does not bar such compensation for past breach.
legal_issues: Whether damages or an account of profits is available without proof of financial loss
Application of Attorney General v Blake to settlement agreement breaches
Appropriate measure for licensing non-Schedule A Hendrix masters
Whether the judge should have made an accounting order instead of accepting an undertaking

linked_authorities.name: Wrotham Park Estate Ltd v Parkside Homes Ltd
Esso Petroleum Co Ltd v Niad Ltd

confidence.notes: Detailed post-Blake remedies judgment; quantification left to later proceedings but principles clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Five IHT settlements or one aggregated settlement
key_facts: Two UK-domiciled brothers each settled property on five parallel discretionary trusts with overseas trustees in 1984.
Company shares were added to each settlement by bonus issues and re-designations; Rysaffe was the current trustee.
HMRC determined that each brother's holdings formed one settlement for ten-year inheritance tax charges, increasing tax compared with five separate settlements.
Park J held there were five settlements per brother; the Court of Appeal dismissed the Revenue's appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by the Commissioners of Inland Revenue from a High Court decision on the number of relevant settlements for periodic IHT charges.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs summarily assessed at £11,750.
enrichment.ratio: Section 43 IHTA defines what constitutes a settlement and what property is comprised in it; where five separate trust deeds each satisfy the definition, there are five settlements under general trust law and section 43 does not permit HMRC to aggregate them by invoking associated operations merely to count settlements for periodic charge purposes.
legal_issues: Construction of settlement in section 43(2) IHTA 1984
Whether associated operations under sections 268 and 272 aggregate parallel trusts into one settlement
How many ten-year IHT charges arise for identical discretionary settlements created by the same settlor
Relationship between general trust law and IHT settlement definition

confidence.notes: Focused statutory construction appeal with unanimous Court of Appeal reasoning.

key_facts: Derek Preston was charged with driving with excess alcohol after a blood specimen showed 119 mg per 100 ml.
Macclesfield justices excluded the blood analysis under section 78 PACE, finding substantial Code C breaches and that he did not comprehend the drink-drive procedure.
The defendant had chronic asthma, diabetes and manic depression but followed the blood procedure and answered medical questions on the proforma.
Mitchell J held there was no evidential basis for exclusion and the decision was Wednesbury unreasonable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Prosecutor's appeal by way of case stated against magistrates' dismissal of a drink-driving charge after exclusion of blood analysis evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to a different bench for rehearing; costs order against respondent not enforceable without leave.
enrichment.ratio: Minor or unsupported alleged breaches of PACE Code C, including failure to call an appropriate adult or police surgeon where the defendant comprehended and consented to the blood procedure, do not justify excluding reliable blood alcohol analysis under section 78; a finding that the defendant failed to comprehend the procedure must be supported by evidence.
legal_issues: Whether Code C paragraphs 1.4, 9.2 and 9.6 were materially breached
Whether the defendant comprehended the drink-drive procedure
Proper exercise of section 78 discretion to exclude blood analysis
Whether magistrates' comprehension finding was supported by evidence

linked_authorities.name: Evans, R (on the application of) v Administrative Court
Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corp

confidence.notes: Full case-stated judgment with detailed fact findings and clear answers to both posed questions.

enrichment.short_title: Demolition condition upheld after land sale
key_facts: The Gosbees obtained outline permission in 1993 for a replacement dwelling on adjoining land subject to demolishing their bungalow Longacre within one month of occupation of the new house.
They sold the development land in 1994; the new dwelling was built but Longacre remained, triggering enforcement proceedings.
A section 73A application to remove condition 2 was refused on appeal; the claimants challenged the inspector's decision under section 288.
Elias J dismissed the claim, holding condition 2 was properly imposed and Article 8 interference proportionate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory challenge under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to an inspector's refusal of a section 73A application to remove a demolition condition.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; claimants ordered to pay the Secretary of State's costs.
enrichment.ratio: A condition requiring demolition of an existing dwelling as part of a one-for-one countryside replacement scheme is lawful and reasonable where retaining both dwellings would undermine rural policy; Article 8 does not require removal of the condition where the claimants voluntarily sold the benefitting land and are authors of their predicament, and an inspector need not consider unrequested alternative conditions.
legal_issues: Whether condition 2 was necessary and reasonably related to the 1993 permission
Whether the condition became unenforceable after sale of part of the site
Materiality of barn conversion history and fallback positions
Whether refusal violated Article 8 ECHR and was disproportionate

linked_authorities.name: R v Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council, ex parte Tew
Newbury District Council v Secretary of State for the Environment
Buckland and Boswell v Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions
R (Samaroo) v Secretary of State for the Home Department

confidence.notes: Comprehensive section 288 judgment addressing planning history, condition law, and human rights.

enrichment.short_title: Land contract variation and section 2 formalities
key_facts: The claimants and defendant entered into an April 2000 contract to sell Mount Pleasant land for £750,000 with completion by 31 July 2000.
After the buyer failed to complete, the parties signed a 17 August 2000 variation increasing the price to £800,000 and extending completion to 14 November 2000.
The buyer again failed to complete; the claimants resold for £675,000 and sued for the shortfall.
The defendant argued the variation was unenforceable because the written consideration for the price increase and delayed completion was not stated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a preliminary issue on whether a varied land sale agreement complied with section 2 of the 1989 Act.
enrichment.ratio: A variation to a land contract that restates parties, property and price in a signed document satisfies section 2 even if it does not expressly narrate the bargain giving rise to each amended term; the agreed price and completion date on the face of the document are sufficient essential elements without spelling out the mutual concessions in longhand.
legal_issues: Whether section 2 requires all expressly agreed terms including consideration for variation to appear in writing
Whether a variation is a new contract subject to full section 2 compliance
Application of McCausland v Duncan Lawrie and Wain v Warlters to land variations

linked_authorities.name: W J Rossiter, George Curtis and others v Daniel Miller

confidence.notes: Focused Chancery preliminary issue with clear section 2 analysis and answer.

enrichment.short_title: GAFTA default date for undelivered sunseed
key_facts: Fleming & Wendeln bought Russian/Ukrainian black sunseed under a GAFTA 78 contract with unfixed price and March 1998 delivery.
Sellers failed to declare loading places and silos by 14 February 1998 and much of the cargo remained undelivered.
Buyers terminated and bought in substitute goods; GAFTA arbitrators held the date of default was 1 March 1998, yielding nominal damages because price-fixing coincided with default.
Cresswell J dismissed the section 69 appeal, applying Toprak v Finagrain to GAFTA 78 clause 28.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 69 appeal with permission on questions of law arising from a GAFTA Board of Appeal award; related section 67 challenge to remitted award.
enrichment.outcome: Section 69 appeal dismissed; section 67 application rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Under GAFTA 78 clause 28, the date of default for assessing damages is the day a main contractual obligation fails, not necessarily the end of the delivery period; where sellers fail to declare loading places and silos—a fundamental step crystallising price and delivery—the default date is that failure (here postponed equitably to 1 March), and later termination does not shift the default date for clause 28(c) purposes.
legal_issues: Meaning of date of default in GAFTA 78 clause 28(c)
Whether buyers could rely on failure to deliver at end of delivery period rather than earlier nomination breach
Application of Toprak v Finagrain to fluid price-fixing contracts
Whether remitted GAFTA award exceeded jurisdiction under section 67

linked_authorities.name: Toprak Mahsulleri Ofisi v Finagrain Compagnie Commerciale Agricole et Financiere SA
Phoebus D Kyprianou Co v Wm H Pim Jr & Co Ltd
Lusograin Export SA v Bunge SA

enrichment.short_title: Strike-out of set-aside for alleged non-disclosure

statutes_considered.title: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975

key_facts: The parties consented at an FDR before Bennett J on 3 August 2001 to a £3.5 million lump sum in full and final settlement of ancillary relief.
The husband later sought to set aside the order alleging the wife fraudulently concealed her relationship and future cohabitation plans with Nick Morris.
Fresh affidavits from acquaintances described conversations about Tuscany and future life together, but the wife denied the thrust of that evidence.
Bennett J struck out the set-aside application as doomed to fail for lack of material non-disclosure and unreasonable delay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Wife's application to strike out the husband's summons to set aside a consent ancillary relief order before the set-aside hearing.
enrichment.ratio: A consent financial remedy order will not be set aside unless absent full and frank disclosure the order would have been substantially different; expressions of future intent and continuing but cooled relationship with a third party do not establish material non-disclosure at the operative FDR date, and Livesey/Barder finality principles filter unmeritorious reopening applications.
legal_issues: Whether the wife materially non-disclosed her relationship with Nick Morris at August 2001
Whether the court would have made a different order with trust restrictions on housing
Application of Livesey v Jenkins and Barder v Barder thresholds
Whether delay barred the set-aside application

confidence.notes: Detailed family procedural judgment applying established non-disclosure and strike-out authorities.
